storyboard.title: How Video Learn writes a lesson
storyboard.summary: What happens between pasting a GitHub link and watching a narrated lesson about it.

scenes.heading: How Video Learn writes a lesson
scenes.subheading: From a GitHub link to a narrated walk through the code
scenes.narration: You paste a link to a repository and ask a question. A couple of minutes later you're watching a lesson about that code. Here's what happens in between, using this app's own code as the example.

scenes.heading: The path of one lesson
scenes.narration: It all starts in one request to the server. First the server downloads the repository. Then Claude reads the code and writes the lesson. Next, every line it cites is checked against the real files. Finally, each scene gets a voice.

scenes.heading: One download, one commit

items.text: The archive names the exact commit
Vendored, binary and huge files are skipped
Source code is kept before docs and tests

scenes.narration: Instead of fetching files one by one, the server downloads the whole repository as a single archive from GitHub. That archive carries the full commit id, so every lesson is tied to one exact version of the code. Vendored folders, binaries and huge files are skipped, and when a repository is too big, source files are kept before docs and tests.

scenes.heading: Claude hands in its work

items.text: Claude submits the lesson as a tool call
The server checks it against the code
Problems go back to Claude to fix

scenes.narration: Claude reads files with three tools, then hands in the finished lesson through a fourth one. The server doesn't just accept it. It checks every file and line range Claude cited, and if something doesn't hold up, the problems go back to Claude to fix and submit again.

scenes.heading: The code on screen is never typed

items.text: Code scenes cite a file and line range
The real lines are copied from the file

scenes.narration: Here's the rule that keeps a lesson honest. Claude never writes the code you see; it only says which file and which lines. The server copies those exact lines out of the repository, so what's on screen is always what's really there.

scenes.heading: Captions that follow the voice
scenes.narration: When ElevenLabs reads a scene aloud, it also returns when each character is spoken. This function groups those characters into words, which is how the captions and the highlighted lines keep pace with the voice.

scenes.heading: What to remember

items.text: Claude cites lines; the server copies them
Word timings keep captions in sync

scenes.narration: So, three things. Each lesson is tied to one exact commit. Claude cites the code and the server copies it, so nothing on screen is invented. And word timings from the voice keep everything in step.
